chapter_summary:
While basic states and transitions are excellent for distinct actions, real-world character animation often requires more nuance, especially for locomotion. This is where **Blend Trees** come into play. A Blend Tree is a special type of state within an Animator Controller that allows you to blend multiple animation clips together based on one or more parameters. This is incredibly powerful for creating smooth, continuous transitions between animations that share a common theme, like varying speeds of movement or different directions.

There are two primary types of Blend Trees:
1.  **1D Blend Tree:** Blends animations along a single parameter. This is perfect for locomotion, where you might blend an "Idle" animation, a "Walk" animation, and a "Run" animation based on a single `Speed` (float) parameter. As the `Speed` parameter increases, the character smoothly transitions from idle to walking, then to running, without needing discrete transitions between each state. To create one, right-click in the Animator window, select "Create State" -> "From New Blend Tree." Double-click the new Blend Tree state to enter its graph. In the Inspector, set the "Blend Type" to "1D." Then, add your animation clips (e.g., Idle, Walk, Run) and define their "Thresholds"—the parameter values at which each animation is fully active. For instance, Idle at `Speed` 0, Walk at `Speed` 0.5, and Run at `Speed` 1. Unity will automatically blend between these.
2.  **2D Blend Tree:** Blends animations based on two parameters, often used for directional movement (e.g., blending forward walk, backward walk, strafe left, strafe right based on `Forward` and `Sideways` parameters). This allows for highly nuanced directional movement. There are several 2D blend types (e.g., Freeform Cartesian, Freeform Directional, Simple Directional), each suitable for different scenarios. For example, Freeform Directional is excellent for blending animations around a central point, like a character turning while moving.

Blend Trees dramatically reduce the complexity of your Animator Controller by replacing numerous individual states and transitions with a single, highly configurable node. They make character movement feel much more organic and responsive.

Beyond blending, characters often need to perform multiple animations simultaneously on different parts of their body. For example, a character might be walking (lower body animation) while simultaneously waving their hand (upper body animation). This is achieved using **Animation Layers**. An Animator Controller can have multiple layers, each running its own state machine. The "Base Layer" is the default and typically handles full-body locomotion. Additional layers can be added for specific body parts or actions.

To add a new layer, go to the "Layers" tab in the Animator window (top-left). Click the "+" button. Each layer has a "Weight" property, which determines its influence (0 to 1). If a layer has a weight of 1, it fully overrides the layers below it for any bones it affects. The key to making layers work together is the **Avatar Mask**. An Avatar Mask is an asset that specifies which bones of the character's rig should be affected by a particular animation layer. For an upper-body waving animation, you would create an Avatar Mask that only includes the spine, chest, shoulders, arms, and hands, leaving the legs and hips unaffected. When you assign this Avatar Mask to your "Upper Body" layer, any animations on that layer will only affect the masked bones, allowing the lower body to continue playing animations from the Base Layer (like walking).

Common mistakes with Blend Trees include setting incorrect thresholds, leading to jerky blends or animations not playing when expected. Always preview your Blend Tree in the Animator window by dragging the parameter slider to ensure smooth transitions. For Animation Layers, a frequent error is forgetting to assign an Avatar Mask, which results in the upper-body animation overriding the entire character, including the legs. Another issue is setting the layer weight incorrectly; if the weight is less than 1, the layer's animations will be blended with the layers below it, which might not be the desired effect for an override layer. Also, ensure that the "Sync" option on a layer is used judiciously. If "Sync" is enabled, the layer will mirror the state machine structure of another layer, which is useful for creating variations (e.g., male and female walk cycles on different layers) but can cause unexpected behavior if not understood. Always test layers and masks thoroughly to ensure the intended body parts are animated.

screens.title: Advanced Mecanim: Blend Trees & Layers
screens.subtitle: Smooth locomotion and partial-body animation using Blend Trees, Layers, and Avatar Masks.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how Mecanim Blend Trees and Animation Layers work together to produce responsive, believable character motion. We’ll focus on two Blend Tree patterns — one‑dimensional blends for speed-based locomotion and two‑dimensional blends for directional movement — and the system that lets you animate the upper body independently using Avatar Masks. You will see how thresholds control which clip is dominant, how layer weight controls influence, and why masks are essential to avoid unintended overrides. A practical hands‑on flow takes you from converting Idle/Walk into a 1D Locomotion Blend Tree to adding a Wave animation on an UpperBody layer, then wiring a script to feed Speed and Trigger parameters. By the end you will understand how to preview blends, diagnose jerky transitions, and apply masks to protect the legs while animating the arms. Think of Blend Trees as a continuous dial and layers with masks as separate control channels; together they let you compose complex behavior without exploding the Animator graph.

keyIdea.title: Main idea
keyIdea.text: Use Blend Trees to interpolate related clips by parameter values, and use Animation Layers plus Avatar Masks to animate different body regions concurrently.

screens.title: What is a Blend Tree?
screens.subtitle: A continuous state that blends multiple clips using parameters

narration.text: A Blend Tree is a special state inside the Animator Controller that blends two or more animation clips based on one or more parameters. That single sentence captures the core: instead of discrete transitions between separate states, a Blend Tree interpolates clips so motion changes smoothly as parameter values change. For example, a Speed parameter can drive a 1D Blend Tree containing Idle at threshold 0, Walk at 0.5, and Run at 1.0. When Speed moves from 0 to 1, the system crossfades and mixes the clips so the character appears to accelerate naturally without explicit transitions between Idle and Walk or Walk and Run. One common misconception is thinking a Blend Tree replaces state logic entirely; it does not — it is itself a state that simplifies related animations. Another misconception is assuming thresholds are automatic; you must set sensible threshold values and preview them. Concrete example: with an analog stick returning a float from the gamepad, feeding that normalized value to Speed yields continuous locomotion. Key takeaway: use Blend Trees to reduce transition complexity and produce organic interpolation, but always test thresholds and preview the blend behavior.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Blend Tree is a state that blends animation clips based on parameters, producing continuous transitions.

content.html:
Core Concept

Blend Tree — definition

A Blend Tree is a single Animator state that interpolates multiple clips based on one or more numeric parameters. It simplifies many similar states into a configurable node.

Why this matters
  • Reduces transitions and conditions in the Animator graph.
  • Makes locomotion and directional movement feel continuous and responsive.
  • Works naturally with analog inputs that produce floats.
Key Takeaway

Treat a Blend Tree as a dial you drive with parameters to blend related clips smoothly.

Illustration: 1D example
Idle
Threshold: 0
Walk
Threshold: 0.5
Run
Threshold: 1.0
Concrete example
Imagine a gamepad returning 0.3 for slow walking. The Blend Tree mixes Idle and Walk so the character lifts feet and leans forward gradually rather than snapping between two poses.
Common mistake
Incorrect thresholds can produce jerky transitions or gaps where no clip is dominant — always preview by dragging the parameter slider.

screens.title: Creating a 1D Locomotion Blend Tree
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: Idle → Walk → Run using a Speed parameter

narration.text: This lesson walks you through building a 1D Blend Tree for locomotion so you can replace discrete Idle and Walk states with a single, continuous node. Start in the Animator window: right-click, Create State → From New Blend Tree, and name it Locomotion. Inside the Blend Tree's inspector set Blend Type to 1D and add a float parameter called Speed in the Parameters tab. Set the Blend Parameter of the tree to Speed. Add three motion fields, assign Idle, Walk, Run clips, and set thresholds to 0, 0.5, and 1 respectively. Return to the Base Layer and set Locomotion as the default state by right‑clicking and choosing Set as Layer Default State. Now normalize your gameplay speed before calling animator. SetFloat so the blend matches thresholds — a common pattern is dividing currentSpeed by a known runSpeed and clamping to 0–1. A common misconception is thinking thresholds must match animation length; thresholds refer to parameter values, not clip durations. After creating the tree, preview it by dragging the Speed slider to confirm a smooth interpolation. Ask yourself: does motion feel natural across typical player inputs?

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Make a Locomotion Blend Tree, add Speed parameter, assign clips, tune thresholds, and set as default state.

content.html:
Process

Build the 1D Blend Tree

1
Create Blend Tree state
Right-click in Animator → Create State → From New Blend Tree. Name it Locomotion.
2
Add Speed parameter
In Parameters tab add a Float named Speed and set the Blend Parameter to Speed.
3
Add clips and thresholds
Add Idle (0), Walk (0.5), Run (1.0). Tune values while previewing the slider.
4
Set default state
Back in Base Layer, right-click Locomotion → Set as Layer Default State.
Validation & example
Normalize your runtime speed before feeding it to the Animator so that 0 maps to Idle and 1 maps to Run. Preview the blend in the Animator by dragging the Speed slider and watching the model. If transitions feel jerky, adjust thresholds and check that clips are authored to blend well.
Concrete code pattern
// Normalize speed example
float normalized = Mathf.Clamp(currentSpeed / runSpeed, 0f, 1f);
animator.SetFloat("Speed", normalized);
Common misconception
Thresholds are parameter values, not clip timing. Setting them wrong causes unexpected blends even with correct clips.

screens.title: 1D vs 2D Blend Trees
screens.subtitle: When to use a single parameter and when to blend with two

narration.text: Knowing when to use a 1D versus a 2D Blend Tree helps you model movement cleanly. A 1D Blend Tree is ideal for variations along a single continuum — speed is the canonical example. If your input is a single float, like an analog trigger or the magnitude of movement input, a 1D tree maps neatly to Idle, Walk, Run thresholds. A 2D Blend Tree is appropriate when two independent parameters determine motion, such as forward and sideways movement for strafing and diagonal motion. It lets you combine directional clips so moving forward-right blends the forward and right strafe animations. There are several 2D blend modes: Freeform Cartesian, Freeform Directional and Simple Directional, each suited to different layouts of clips in parameter space. A common error is using a 1D tree to approximate directional movement, which forces awkward workarounds. Another pitfall is misplacing clips in the 2D graph so some directions lack coverage. Concrete example: use a 2D Freeform Directional tree when you have distinct forward, backward, left, and right clips and want smooth steering. Question to reflect on: which parameter set best represents the player’s control scheme?

keyIdea.title: Choose the right blend
keyIdea.text: 1D for single continua like speed; 2D for combining orthogonal controls such as forward and sideways movement.

content.html:
Comparison

1D Blend Tree

Best for a single control value like speed. Simple to set up and easy to tune thresholds.

Example
Idle (0) → Walk (0.5) → Run (1.0) driven by Speed.
Comparison

2D Blend Tree

Use when two parameters, typically forward and sideways, determine which animation blend to play. Choose the 2D blend type that fits how clips are laid out.

Example
Forward, Backward, Strafe Left, Strafe Right blended by Forward and Sideways floats.
Common mistake
Using 1D when your controls are directional forces awkward crossfades and incomplete movement coverage.

screens.title: Thresholds and Previewing Blends
screens.subtitle: How thresholds steer which clip dominates and how to verify them

narration.text: Thresholds are numeric parameter values assigned to each motion in a Blend Tree that define when that motion should be fully active. They don't control timing of the clip; they only indicate the parameter value where the clip is most influential. For a 1D tree with Idle at 0, Walk at 0.5, and Run at 1.0, setting the correct numeric thresholds is essential for natural-feeling transitions. Always preview by dragging the Blend Parameter slider in the Animator window — this reveals how clips weight against each other across the parameter range. A practical example: If your player's analog stick produces values mainly between 0.2 and 0.6 during typical play, placing Walk centered at 0.5 works well, while Idle remains near 0. If thresholds are wrong, you can see jerks or moments where motion seems to freeze because two clips compete poorly. A frequent misconception is to match thresholds to animation energy rather than to expected input values; thresholds must reflect runtime parameters. Final check: test with real input ranges, not just theoretical extremes. Thresholds and Previewing Blends means thresholds map parameter values to clip dominance; preview and tune them using real input ranges for smooth blending.. In practical terms, how thresholds steer which clip dominates and how to verify them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Thresholds
keyIdea.text: Thresholds map parameter values to clip dominance; preview and tune them using real input ranges for smooth blending.

content.html:
Definition

Thresholds

Assign numeric values to motion fields so the Blend Tree knows which clip should be active at which parameter value.

Preview tip
Use the Animator’s parameter slider to scrub values and observe clip weights in real time. Make adjustments while watching the character for smoothness.
Example scenario
A twin-stick control scheme often produces small input magnitudes while aiming; map your Walk threshold to the most frequent walking magnitude rather than averaging extremes.
Mistake to avoid
Don’t base thresholds on clip names or perceived energy. Base them on measured input ranges from playtesting to avoid unnatural blends.
Try this

Record joystick values during play and use the distribution to place thresholds where the player actually spends time.

screens.title: Animation Layers Explained
screens.subtitle: Run independent state machines and combine results with layer weight

narration.text: Animation Layers let you compose multiple Animator state machines that run in parallel. The Base Layer typically controls full‑body locomotion. Additional layers can contain their own states and transitions, allowing you to play actions like waving or reloading on top of locomotion without rebuilding the Base Layer. Each layer has a Weight value from 0 to 1 that governs how strongly it influences the final pose. When a layer is assigned an Avatar Mask, only the masked bones are affected by that layer. For example, an UpperBody layer with a weight of 1 and a mask selecting chest and arms will fully override those bones while leaving the legs to the Base Layer. A common misconception is that layers automatically target specific bones — without a mask, a layer will affect the whole skeleton and may unintentionally override the Base Layer. Practical tip: set Weight to 1 for a full override of masked bones and preview combined results in the Animator to ensure interactions are correct. Animation Layers Explained means use layers to run separate state machines and control influence via weight and masks to compose partial-body animations.. In practical terms, run independent state machines and combine results with layer weight. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Layer purpose
keyIdea.text: Use layers to run separate state machines and control influence via weight and masks to compose partial-body animations.

content.html:
Core Concept

Animation Layers

Layers let you run multiple state machines in parallel and blend their results. They are ideal for overlaying actions like aim, wave, or reload on top of locomotion.

Layer Weight
Weight controls influence. A value of 1 fully applies the layer to its masked bones; less than 1 blends with lower layers.
Example: UpperBody layer
Create a new layer named UpperBody, set Weight to 1, assign an Avatar Mask that selects spine, chest, shoulders, arms and hands, then add a Wave state to that layer. Trigger it via a WaveTrigger parameter.
Common pitfall
Forgetting an Avatar Mask makes the layer affect the whole skeleton, causing leg animations to stop when the upper body plays an action.

screens.title: Creating an Avatar Mask
screens.subtitle: Select bones to isolate layer influence

narration.text: An Avatar Mask specifies which bones an animation layer will affect. Creating one is straightforward but requires careful selection. In the Project window create → Avatar Mask and open it in the Inspector. Choose Humanoid and expand the skeleton tree. For an UpperBody mask deselect bones below the spine — typically Hips, UpperLeg, LowerLeg, Foot, and Toes — and ensure Spine, Chest, Shoulders, Arms, and Hands are selected. Apply your changes and then assign the Avatar Mask to the UpperBody layer’s Mask slot. Set the layer Weight to 1 if you want the masked bones fully overridden. A common error is deselecting a bone you actually need, producing subtle animation gaps, or forgetting to apply the mask so it doesn’t take effect. After assignment, test by playing the scene and triggering the upper-body animation while locomotion runs. If legs stop moving, inspect the mask and layer weight; this usually indicates a mask problem or an unintended full-body animation on the layer. Creating an Avatar Mask means avatar masks restrict which bones a layer animates, enabling partial-body overrides like waving while walking.. In practical terms, select bones to isolate layer influence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avatar Mask
keyIdea.text: Avatar Masks restrict which bones a layer animates, enabling partial-body overrides like waving while walking.

content.html:
Process

Create Avatar Mask

  1. Create → Avatar Mask in Project window.
  2. In Inspector choose Humanoid and expand skeleton.
  3. Deselect lower body bones; select spine, chest, shoulders, arms, hands.
  4. Assign mask to layer Mask slot and set Weight appropriately.
Validation
After assignment, play a Wave animation on the UpperBody layer and confirm the Base Layer locomotion continues on the legs. If the legs stop, check that the mask actually has lower bones deselected and the layer contains only upper-body states.
Gotcha
An avatar mask will not fix an animation that already animates the entire skeleton — ensure the clip itself targets only the bones you intend, or use masks and retargeted clips.

screens.title: Layer Weight and Sync Options
screens.subtitle: Influence and mirroring behavior between layers

narration.text: Layer Weight controls how much influence an animation layer has on the final pose. When Weight equals 1, the layer fully applies its animations to masked bones; when less than 1, Unity blends the layer results with lower layers. Use weights less than one for subtle additive effects or partial overrides. Sync is an option that makes a layer mirror the state machine structure of another layer so states can progress in lockstep. Sync is useful when you want variations of the same motion on different layers, for example slightly different walk cycles for different equipment. A common misuse is enabling Sync without understanding the mirrored structure — this will force the synced layer to follow state changes from the target layer and may produce unexpected state changes. A practical example: set UpperBody Weight to 1 for a distinct wave; set a secondary gesture layer to 0.3 to add breathing movement on top of full-body cycles. Always test combinations to ensure intended dominance and timing. Layer Weight and Sync Options means use weight for influence and sync to mirror state progression; test both to avoid unexpected overrides.. In practical terms, influence and mirroring behavior between layers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Layer controls
keyIdea.text: Use Weight for influence and Sync to mirror state progression; test both to avoid unexpected overrides.

content.html:
Comparison

Weight: influence control

Weight = 1 fully applies layer to masked bones. Weight < 1 blends with layers below. Use lower weights for additive subtle motions, and full weight when overriding masked bones is required.
Sync option
Enable Sync to mirror the structure and timing of another layer. Useful for variations of the same state machine but dangerous if you want independent timing.
Common mistake
Turning on Sync unintentionally ties the layer lifecycle to another layer’s states, which can cause unexpected transitions.

screens.title: Add UpperBody Layer and Wave State
screens.subtitle: Create a masked layer and trigger a transient upper-body action

narration.text: This lesson covers adding an UpperBody layer and wiring a Wave animation triggered at runtime. In the Animator window go to the Layers tab and click the plus button to add a new layer. Name it UpperBody and drag your Avatar Mask into the Mask slot. Set Weight to 1 so masked bones are fully affected. In the UpperBody layer’s graph drag a Wave clip to create a Wave state. Create a Trigger parameter named WaveTrigger in Parameters. From Any State create a transition to Wave, uncheck Has Exit Time, and add WaveTrigger as the condition. From Wave create a transition back to Entry or Exit and set Has Exit Time true with a short transition duration (0.2) so the animation resumes to its rest pose. A common misconception is relying on Exit rather than designing a clean return path; ensure your Wave state returns properly so the layer doesn’t become stuck. Test by firing WaveTrigger at runtime and watching the upper body wave while legs continue to play locomotion from the Base Layer. Add UpperBody Layer and Wave State means add a layer, assign avatar mask, create wave state, add wavetrigger and transitions, and test runtime behavior.. In practical terms, create a masked layer and trigger a transient upper-body action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UpperBody layer setup
keyIdea.text: Add a layer, assign Avatar Mask, create Wave state, add WaveTrigger and transitions, and test runtime behavior.

content.html:
Steps
  1. Add new layer in Layers tab and name it UpperBody.
  2. Assign the Avatar Mask to the layer Mask slot and set Weight to 1.
  3. Add Wave clip as a state and create WaveTrigger in Parameters.
  4. Transition Any State → Wave with condition WaveTrigger and no Exit Time.
  5. From Wave set a transition back with Has Exit Time true and short duration.
Testing checklist
  • Press the configured input to fire the trigger and observe the upper body only.
  • Confirm base locomotion continues on the legs while Wave plays.
  • If legs stop, inspect the Avatar Mask and layer Weight settings.
Pro tip

Use short transition durations for transient actions to keep animation flow responsive.

screens.title: PlayerMovementAnimator Script
screens.subtitle: Drive Speed and trigger WaveTrigger from input

narration.text: The PlayerMovementAnimator script connects player input to the Animator parameters so the Blend Tree and UpperBody layer respond to gameplay. The provided script grabs horizontal and vertical axes to build a movement vector and computes its magnitude as currentSpeed. It applies a run multiplier when Left Shift is held, then normalizes that value against runSpeed before setting the Speed float on the animator, which drives the 1D Blend Tree thresholds. The script also checks for a Space key press and sets the WaveTrigger to fire the UpperBody wave. Note a common issue: forgetting to clamp or normalize the Speed value can push thresholds out of range, producing unexpected blends. Another potential pitfall is calling SetTrigger without confirming the Animator reference is valid; the Start method logs an error if Animator is missing. Concrete example: runSpeed=3f, walkSpeed=1.5f — normalize by dividing currentSpeed by runSpeed and clamp between 0 and 1. Test movement and wave trigger together to validate layered behavior. What change would you make to preserve root motion instead of moving the transform manually? PlayerMovementAnimator Script means normalize runtime speed for the blend tree and fire trigger parameters to control layered animations.. In practical terms, drive speed and trigger wavetrigger from input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script role
keyIdea.text: Normalize runtime speed for the Blend Tree and fire trigger parameters to control layered animations.

content.html:
Code

PlayerMovementAnimator (excerpt)

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovementAnimator : MonoBehaviour
{
    private Animator animator;
    public float walkSpeed = 1.5f;
    public float runSpeed = 3f;

    void Start()
    {
        animator = GetComponent();
        if (animator == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("Animator component not found on this GameObject!");
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        float verticalInput = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector3 movementInput = new Vector3(horizontalInput, 0, verticalInput);
        float currentSpeed = movementInput.magnitude;

        // Determine if walking or running
        if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.LeftShift))
        {
            currentSpeed *= runSpeed; // Apply run speed multiplier
        }
        else
        {
            currentSpeed *= walkSpeed; // Apply walk speed multiplier
        }

        // Set the Speed parameter in the Animator (clamped to 0-1 for blend tree thresholds)
        animator.SetFloat("Speed", Mathf.Clamp0(currentSpeed / runSpeed, 0f, 1f)); // Normalize speed for blend tree

        // Optional: Basic character movement (if not using Root Motion for movement)
        if (!animator.applyRootMotion)
        {
            Vector3 movement = movementInput.normalized * currentSpeed * Time.deltaTime;
            transform.position += movement;
            if (movementInput.magnitude > 0)
            {
                transform.rotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(movementInput);
            }
        }

        // Trigger wave animation
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            animator.SetTrigger("WaveTrigger");
        }
    }
}
Explanation & checks
  • Normalize currentSpeed by runSpeed to align with Blend Tree thresholds.
  • Clamp values to 0–1 to prevent thresholds being exceeded.
  • Use applyRootMotion to decide if the Animator drives movement or if you move the transform manually.
  • Always verify animator is not null to avoid runtime errors when calling SetFloat or SetTrigger.
Reflection

If you use Root Motion, disable the manual transform update and let the animation drive displacement for more accurate foot placement.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips
screens.subtitle: Diagnose jerky blends, incorrect masks, and layer conflicts

narration.text: Debugging Blend Trees and layers is mostly about inspecting parameter ranges, thresholds, masks, and transitions. If blends feel jerky, first open the Blend Tree and drag the parameter slider to see clip weights across the range — jerks usually indicate thresholds placed too close or clips with mismatched root motion or timings. If an upper-body animation overrides the legs, the most likely cause is a missing or misconfigured Avatar Mask; open the mask and verify lower body bones are deselected. If a layer doesn’t fully apply, check the layer Weight — values less than one will blend the layer with lower layers. For unexpected timing issues, inspect the Sync option; disabling it allows independent timing. Also verify Animator parameter values are being set as expected at runtime by watching the Animator’s Parameters inspector while the game runs. Concrete example: if pressing Space to wave freezes leg movement, watch whether WaveTrigger has been set and whether the UpperBody layer has a mask; this typically points directly to a mask or weight error. Final question: which inspector view will show you live parameter values while the game plays?

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Use the Animator preview and live parameter view to find threshold, mask, or weight errors causing incorrect blends.

content.html:
Symptoms & Causes
  • Jerky blends — thresholds too close or clip mismatch.
  • Upper body overrides legs — missing or wrong Avatar Mask.
  • Layer not applied fully — Weight < 1 or incorrect mask scope.
  • Unexpected transitions — Sync enabled or conditions misconfigured.
Practical checks
  1. Preview Blend Tree slider and watch clip weights.
  2. Play the scene and inspect Animator Parameters live.
  3. Open Avatar Mask and confirm bone selections.
  4. Check layer Weight and Sync settings.
Key Takeaway

Systematically inspect parameter values, masks, and weights to isolate animation conflicts quickly.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Assemble Locomotion + Upper Body Wave
screens.subtitle: Follow the lab steps to implement the full system and test behaviors

narration.text: This lab pulls together everything you’ve learned. Prepare Idle, Walk, Run, and Wave clips. Create a 1D Blend Tree named Locomotion and add Speed parameter with thresholds 0, 0.5, 1. Create an Avatar Mask named UpperBodyMask selecting spine, chest, shoulders, arms, and hands. Add an UpperBody layer, set Weight to 1, and assign the mask. Add Wave state to the UpperBody layer, create WaveTrigger, and make a transition from Any State to Wave with Has Exit Time unchecked and WaveTrigger as the condition. Normalize runtime speed in your PlayerMovementAnimator script and set the Speed float. Test movement and confirm the Wave trigger fires while legs keep playing locomotion. While running the lab watch for jerky blends, verify thresholds, and ensure the mask is applied. This lab approach helps you iteratively build, test, and adjust so the final result is a responsive character that walks or runs and can perform upper-body actions without breaking locomotion. After completing the steps, reflect: what small threshold change made the biggest improvement in feel? keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: A normalized Speed feeding a 1D Blend Tree plus a masked UpperBody layer gives layered, responsive animation.

content.html:
Lab Steps
  1. Prepare clips: Idle, Walk, Run, Wave.
  2. Create Locomotion 1D Blend Tree; add Speed parameter and thresholds 0, 0.5, 1.
  3. Create Avatar Mask UpperBodyMask and select upper bones only.
  4. Add UpperBody layer, set Weight=1, assign the mask, add Wave state and WaveTrigger.
  5. Wire PlayerMovementAnimator to set Speed and trigger WaveTrigger on input.
  6. Play and test: adjust thresholds and mask selections as needed.
Checkpoints
  • Blend Tree preview shows smooth transitions.
  • UpperBody wave plays while legs continue walking.
  • No unintended full-body overrides occur when WaveTrigger fires.
Why it matters

This lab teaches composition: blending related motions with Blend Trees and composing independent actions using layers and masks for scalable, maintainable Animator graphs.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember about Blend Trees, Layers, and Masks

narration.text: Let’s summarize the essential concepts. First, a Blend Tree is a state that blends multiple animation clips using numeric parameters; use 1D for single continua like speed and 2D for directional movement. Second, thresholds map parameter values to clip dominance; tune them with the Animator preview slider and base thresholds on real input ranges. Third, Animation Layers allow independent state machines that can be blended according to Layer Weight. Fourth, Avatar Masks restrict which bones a layer affects, enabling partial‑body overrides like waving while walking. Keep in mind common mistakes: wrong thresholds produce jerky blends, missing masks allow unintended full‑body overrides, and incorrect layer weight or sync settings produce unexpected behavior. Practice building a Locomotion Blend Tree and adding an UpperBody masked layer, then connect a runtime script that normalizes speed and triggers upper‑body actions. These building blocks let you design complex, composable character behaviors without exploding the Animator graph.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Blend Trees for continuous motion, Layers for parallel state machines, and Avatar Masks for targeted bone control.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Key Concepts
Blend Tree
A state that blends clips by parameter values for continuous transitions.
Animation Layer
An independent state machine that can run parallel to the Base Layer and blend by weight.
Avatar Mask
An asset that specifies which bones an animation layer will affect, enabling partial overrides.
Summary

Combine normalized runtime parameters with Blend Trees and use masked layers for composed, responsive character animation.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for everyday use

narration.text: Here are three compact reminders to carry into your next project. First, always normalize and clamp your runtime values before feeding them to a Blend Tree so thresholds behave predictably. Second, use Avatar Masks whenever a layer should affect only part of the skeleton — this prevents accidental full‑body overrides. Third, preview everything in the Animator: drag blend parameters, inspect live parameter values while the game runs, and test transitions and layer weights together. These small habits prevent the most common problems and make iteration faster. As you implement the locomotion blend and an upper‑body layer, keep these checks in mind to verify each step and to ensure your character behaves consistently under player control. What to Remember means normalize inputs, mask layers correctly, and preview parameters during runtime to catch issues early.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for everyday use. keyIdea.title: Quick reminders
keyIdea.text: Normalize inputs, mask layers correctly, and preview parameters during runtime to catch issues early.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Quick Reference
Normalize & Clamp
Ensure input maps correctly to Blend Tree thresholds by normalizing and clamping values.
Mask bones precisely
Select only the bones needed so a layer affects just the intended body parts.
Preview & Test
Use Animator previews and live parameter inspection during play to verify blends and layer interactions.
Final takeaway

Blend Trees and Layers are powerful when used together; consistent testing and masking practices keep animations stable and composable.
